content:
Holding on until the last moment

"To be frank, we held on until the very last moment." Ms. Yuen and her younger sister grew up at Wang Fuk Court with their parents. After their father passed away and her elder sister moved out after marriage, Ms. Yuen lived with her mother alone until the fire. Her mother died in the blaze. In the past, when going upstairs, she once wore a sweater with the handwritten slogan "Redevelop in-situ" to express her demands. But the authorities rejected the proposal and the owners' corporation refused to put it on the agenda. It was only one week before the acquisition deadline of 31 August that she submitted a letter accepting the acquisition offer.

Ms. Yuen believes the Wang Fuk Court residents have been 'caught between a rock and a hard place.' She said the two explanation officers she had dealt with were unable to answer her questions, and their only clear objective was to press residents on whether they had sold their flats.

Post-disaster life is 'just staying over'

Since the fire, Ms. Yuen has stayed at Shin Lau in Tai Po and later moved to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a 'temporary residence fee' every month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet that came with the unit, as well as the neighbours and security guards, constantly remind her of her status. She describes her life after the incident as 'just staying over'.

Rethinking what 'home' and 'family' mean

She finishes work and returns to this empty flat at eight or nine o'clock every day. On holidays she chooses to leave and go to her sister's place. 'Actually, after the incident, I started thinking about what is meant by "home," what is meant by "residence." A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when the home of Wang Fuk Court can be burned down like that...'

The word 'home' has become quite heavy for me

When the reporter asked Ms. Yuen about her vision of home, she said the old phone containing photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories remain only in her mind. She sighed and said, "Home is not simply about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, and a full set of home appliances to make it a so-called proper home. It makes me rethink what the elements of a proper home really are, so I can't answer this question for now, because the word 'home' has become quite heavy for me."

Resentment over officials' 'letting go' remarks

The responses of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire—such as Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing's remarks about 'letting go' and Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun's references to market value—have added to her helplessness and anger. 'The more silent you are, the less I understand,' she said. 'When they can actually say such callous things, what does home mean to them in their minds?'

A feeling of selling at a knockdown price

Ms. Yuen recalled that the strongest feeling at the moment of signing the letter accepting the acquisition was unwillingness and a sense of injustice—a feeling of selling at a knockdown price, because home is not just real estate value but also emotional and memory ties. 'This unit is something my dad and mum worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken from us as if it has no value, rather than this "knockdown sale," I feel even more unwilling.'

After signing the letter, Ms. Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has been delayed until October to submit its report. Ms. Yuen said holding people accountable is part of it, 'but as for how I personally move forward, I can't answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss—first, the home was burned down, and the burning means, as it were, wiping away the history of my growing up. A family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death... There's a big hole in my heart. Can this hole really be filled? Or will it one day heal? I don't know how to answer.'
